scenes.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service
scenes.narration: This slide introduces Amazon OpenSearch Service as the managed AWS search and analytics offering. Begin with the sources on the left: documents, logs and optional event data enter through batch or streaming ingestion. The central OpenSearch indexes organise those records so they can be queried efficiently. Follow the three branches on the right. Full-text search finds relevant text in indexed documents. Analytics dashboards visualise and explore time-series or other indexed data. Vector search can support semantic retrieval for generative AI when embeddings are stored in the index. Now examine the lower comparison. An OpenSearch index is a searchable representation of information, while a relational database such as Amazon RDS is designed around transactional storage and queries. OpenSearch is not normally the source of truth for frequent transactional updates. Start an architecture decision by asking whether the workload prioritizes fast text search, log exploration, analytics or semantic retrieval.

scenes.title: What Is OpenSearch?
scenes.narration: Let's separate the core search engine from the AWS service that manages it. The flow across the slide begins with logs, application data and other sources. Those records are ingested as indexed documents. A user then issues a search or analytics query, and the engine returns matching results or aggregated values. The right-hand example shows search fields and charts built from that indexed content. In the comparison at the bottom, OpenSearch is the underlying open-source search and analytics engine. Amazon OpenSearch Service is the managed AWS service that helps create and operate OpenSearch deployments, including infrastructure, deployment configuration and some operational tasks. The managed service does not remove responsibility for mappings, permissions, index design, shard sizing and query performance. When an exam scenario asks for near-real-time log search or full-text discovery, OpenSearch may fit well. When the primary need is ACID transactions, look elsewhere.

scenes.title: OpenSearch Dashboards
scenes.narration: OpenSearch Dashboards is the visual interface built around indexed data. The numbered process at the top starts by loading and indexing source documents. Next, an analyst builds a saved search with the relevant fields and filters. A visualization turns query results into charts or tables, and finally those visuals are combined into a dashboard. Look at the example beneath the steps. A log-volume line chart and an error-count bar chart show different perspectives of the same monitored system. The lower list highlights common error messages to help the analyst investigate the increase. Notice that a dashboard is a layer over search results; it does not create missing data or guarantee the index is current. To build a useful operational dashboard, first confirm ingestion, timestamp mappings, data permissions and query filters. Then choose visuals that answer a question, such as whether errors are increasing and which events caused them.

scenes.title: OpenSearch Applications
scenes.narration: The same indexed data can support several different applications, and this slide shows five branches from one OpenSearch cluster. The sources on the left include documents, application logs, metrics, security events and user events. The first branch is full-text document search, such as finding a manual that mentions a specific equipment fault. The second is log analytics, where teams search and filter application or infrastructure logs. The third is application monitoring, measuring latency or requests over time. The fourth branch is security analytics, which may identify suspicious account or network activity. Finally, clickstream analysis helps understand which pages or actions people use before a process completes. The important architectural point is that the same engine can be used for different query patterns, but that does not imply one giant undifferentiated index is best. Design separate mappings, retention periods, access controls and capacities to match the workload.

scenes.title: Documents, Mappings and Indices
scenes.narration: This slide defines three core OpenSearch concepts. On the left, a document is a JSON record with an identifier and fields. The examples are log events, each with a timestamp, severity and message. Follow the arrows into the centre index: an index groups these searchable documents so the engine can retrieve matching records. On the right, field mappings define how individual fields are interpreted. Notice that the timestamp has a date type, severity is a keyword and message is analysed as text. That distinction changes the queries you can execute efficiently: an exact filter on severity behaves differently from a full-text search of the message. The three documents on the left illustrate why a consistent mapping matters. If a timestamp is accidentally indexed as a string or a numeric field changes type, searches and aggregations can fail or behave unexpectedly. Choose mappings before a large ingestion when possible, and validate real sample records.

scenes.title: An Index Is Split into Shards
scenes.narration: An OpenSearch index is divided into shards to distribute data and query work. Look at the document IDs entering from the far left. A routing process determines which primary shard stores each document. The diagram shows three primary shards distributed across nodes, with replica copies available on other nodes. Follow the search query from the top into the eligible shard copies. Search operations can run across relevant shards, and the results are combined before they return to the application. That's why the final box is labelled merge results. Sharding improves distributed capacity, but every shard consumes resources and adds coordination overhead. It is not automatically better to create the largest possible shard count. In a production design, consider how many documents will be indexed, query frequency, node resources, and recovery time before choosing shard configuration.

scenes.title: Primary Shards and Replicas
scenes.narration: This slide separates two important OpenSearch responsibilities: writes and reads. Start at the top-left write request. It reaches the assigned primary shard, shown in orange, and the operation is then replicated to replica copies on other nodes. The purple copies are useful because they can serve searches and provide availability when a node fails. Now look at the read request below. A read can be served by an eligible primary or replica, so replicas can contribute to read capacity as well as resilience. The right-hand panel lists the benefits: availability, query capacity and distributed placement. But the large red note says replicas are not backups. A corrupted record or accidental deletion may be replicated too, so snapshots are still necessary for recovery. When reviewing this architecture, also check fault-domain distribution and the number of shards per node so one failed server doesn't eliminate all copies.
